# Testing a model's calibration yourself {#sec-ch09}

::: {.epigraph by="Russian proverb, made famous by Ronald Reagan, 1987"}
Trust, but verify.
:::

A week after Jev launched, two claims were going round. TypeSafe's: Jev returns *calibrated* probabilities [@typesafe2026]. And a reply from the data scientist Alex Molas, titled "Jev can't be calibrated": treat its outputs as scores, because calibration depends on *your* data, and Jev never sees your data [@molas2026]. Which is right? Both, in a precise sense, and you can settle it for your own use in an afternoon.

::: {.goals}
- Explain why calibration depends on your data.
- Fix a base-rate mismatch with a few hundred labels.
- Know how many labels a calibration check needs.
:::

## Why the critic has a point

A probability is a claim about *how often, among cases like this one* (Chapter 2). Two companies send the same alert text; the model reads the same input and returns the same number to both. But if one company is attacked often and the other rarely, the true share of attacks among alerts like this differs between them. One number can't be right for both.

This is the base-rate trap again, now catching the model. A model tuned on one mix of outcomes can be perfectly calibrated there and wrong in the same direction everywhere the mix differs.

::: {.keyidea}
Calibration is a property of a model *and the data it's used on*.
:::

![The same model's reliability at two companies. At Kestrel, whose mix of alerts matches what the stand-in was built around, it sits close to the diagonal. At Harbor, where attacks are rarer, every probability is too high.](/figures/ch18/two-companies.pdf){#fig-two-companies}

To show it, I made a second synthetic company, Harbor Pharma: same detectors, same-looking alerts, but rarer attacks ({{< num ch18 harbor_base pct1 >}} against {{< num ch18 kestrel_base pct1 >}}). The same model's calibration error is {{< num ch18 ece_kestrel f3 >}} at Kestrel and {{< num ch18 ece_harbor f3 >}} at Harbor, always in the same direction: Harbor's average predicted risk is {{< num ch18 harbor_mean_p pct1 >}} against a real rate of {{< num ch18 harbor_base pct1 >}} (@fig-two-companies). Nothing about the model changed. Only the world did.

## Fixing it

This kind of error is often easy to fix. If the probabilities were right for one base rate and you know yours, adjust the odds by the ratio of the two: Bayes' rule again, with only the starting point moved [@saerens2002]. With the base rate known, Harbor's ECE falls to {{< num ch18 ece_prior_known f3 >}}. **Platt scaling** fitted on just 300 of Harbor's labelled alerts does even better: {{< num ch18 ece_platt300 f3 >}}. It can also fix probabilities that are too spread out or too bunched, not only too high.

![Harbor's alerts, on the cases not used for fitting: as returned (red, solid line), after adjusting the odds for Harbor's base rate (blue, dashed line), and after Platt scaling on 300 labelled alerts (green, dotted line). Both fixes bring the curve most of the way back to the diagonal.](/figures/ch18/harbor-fixes.pdf){#fig-harbor-fixes}

## How many labels?

![The ECE you'd measure from a random sample of labelled alerts, for different sample sizes, on a model whose ECE over all 20,000 alerts is shown by the labelled black horizontal line. With a hundred labels the measurement is both noisy and too high on average: a calibrated model looks miscalibrated. The error shrinks as samples grow.](/figures/ch18/ece-noise.pdf){#fig-ece-noise}

Small samples badly mislead calibration measurements. The stand-in's true ECE across 20,000 alerts is {{< num ch18 ece_full f3 >}}. Measured on a random 100 labelled alerts, the typical result is {{< num ch18 ece_n100 f3 >}}, over three times too high, and one sample in twenty says {{< num ch18 ece_n100_hi f3 >}} (@fig-ece-noise). With few cases per group, each group's rate jumps around by chance, and ECE adds up the *size* of those jumps whatever their direction, so noise always pushes it up.

::: {.keyidea}
With few labels, ECE is biased upwards. Report a range, and don't call a model miscalibrated on a hundred cases.
:::

Rule of thumb: a few hundred labels are enough to *fix* a big error that always goes the same way; a few thousand to *confirm* calibration within a point or two.

For pick-one questions, start by checking the top label: when its confidence is around 0.8, is it right about 80% of the time? The stand-in's top category averages {{< num ch18 top_conf_mean pct >}} confidence and is right {{< num ch18 top_acc pct >}} of the time. Then check the labels you actually act on.

![Top-label calibration for the category question on 2,500 of Kestrel's alerts: the confidence of the model's top category against how often that category was right.](/figures/ch18/top-label.pdf){#fig-top-label}

## A routine you can repeat

1. **Collect labels** from recent cases with settled outcomes, including a random sample of cases the machine closed itself, or you'll only ever label what people looked at.
2. **Plot, don't just score.** A reliability diagram with the counts showing, and ECE with a range. Look hardest near your thresholds.
3. **Slice** by every group you treat differently.
4. **Fix**: a base-rate adjustment if that's the problem, otherwise Platt or temperature scaling on your labels.
5. **Repeat** on a schedule, and whenever the model version or your data changes.

![A testing routine for any model that returns probabilities, Jev included.](/figures/ch18/protocol.pdf){#fig-protocol}

So: the vendor may well be right that Jev is calibrated on the data they tested. The critic is right that this doesn't make it calibrated on yours. The routine turns the argument into a measurement.

::: {.keyidea}
Treat a new model's outputs as scores until you've tested them on your own data.
:::

::: {.breaks}
Labels aren't perfect. People disagree, some attacks are never found, and outcomes arrive late: an alert closed today may belong to a break-in found next month. Measure on "mature" labels whose outcomes have settled. And beware labels that exist only because of the model's own decisions: if it auto-closed a case, nobody labelled it.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. You have 150 labelled cases and measure ECE 0.05. A colleague says the model is badly calibrated. What would you say, and do?
:::
